newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish to send minister to Russia over beef exports.
newsitem.headline: Irish to send minister to Russia over beef exports.

text.p: Irish agriculture minister Ivan Yates said on Thursday he planned an early visit to Moscow to try to overturn Russia's ban on beef imports from three Irish counties because of concern over mad cow disease.

Yates on Tuesday signed an agreement with Russia, Ireland's biggest single export market for beef, to prevent beef from the counties of Cork, Tipperary and Monaghan being exported to Russia with effect from November 1.
He said Russia had threatened a complete ban on Irish beef because of fears that Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) could be transmitted to humans.

Ireland instead accepted a selective agreement stopping exports from the three counties, and this ban would be reviewed by Russia in three months if the number of new Irish BSE cases fell, Yates said.
"The decision was taken with the greatest reluctance," he told Ireland's parliament during a special debate on the deal with Russia.
"However the stark choice we were facing was the closure of the Russian market to all Irish beef or the exclusion of three counties on a temporary basis."

The agreement provoked fury amongst Irish farmers and opposition politicians, who said it would damage international confidence in Irish beef and encourage other countries to introduce similar selective bans.
"Government policy on beef is now in tatters," said Irish Farmers Association President John Donnelly. "The concession that minister Yates made to the Russians does untold damage."
Donnelly said urgent political action was required to restore confidence in Irish beef across the world.
Ireland says its beef is safe to eat and insists it has strict policies to deal with BSE. The country has reported 153 cases of BSE, including 40 in Cork, eight in Tipperary and five in Monaghan.
Yates said there was no scientific justification for Russia's selective ban and he would not accept similar selective bans from other countries.
But he said the number of BSE cases in Ireland, while low, had doubled in 1996.
"There have been 38 cases of BSE in Ireland in 1996 to date, which is more than double the number in 1995 and is higher than the level in any year to date," he told parliament.
